kurals.tamil:
கருமத்தால் நாணுதல் நாணுந் திருநுதல்
நல்லவர் நாணுப் பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Karumaththaal naanudhal naanum thirunudhal
nallavar naanup pira.
kurals.meaning: True shame is shrinking back from a wrong deed; the other kinds of bashfulness are the natural modesty of graceful, bright-browed women.
kurals.elementary: Some kids feel shy when they have to sing in front of the class; that is one kind of shy. But Valluvar says the shame that really matters is the feeling that stops your hand just before you do something mean or wrong. That feeling is like a good friend inside you.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by defining its subject: naanudhal (நாணுதல், 'shrinking, being abashed') that arises karumaththaal (கருமத்தால், 'on account of a deed'), i.e. recoiling from a base act, is the naan (நாண்) of the good. Puliyur Kesikan, following the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, glosses the second line as saying that the other shrinkings of mind, speech and body are the modesty proper to women of good family (thirunudhal nallavar, 'the good ones of beautiful brow'), so Valluvar separates a moral emotion open to everyone from a customary, gendered bashfulness. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope renders the moral sense as ‘generous shame’. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101) and before Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103), the chapter treats naan as the inner guard of the well-born person. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh writes the same words; only spacing differs).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hrī means that one should be very modest and must not perform some act which is abominable.”
hinduism.explanation: Commenting on the list of divine qualities in Gita 16.1-3, Prabhupada defines hrī, modesty, as the refusal to do anything abominable.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own definition: real shame is recoiling from a base deed.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3, purport (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the wording is the translator's purport, not the verse itself, but the verse lists hrīḥ among the divine qualities.

christianity.quote_or_event: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
christianity.explanation: Joseph refuses the advances of Potiphar's wife, recoiling from the act itself rather than from the risk of being caught.
christianity.tie_back: Joseph's recoil is the ‘shame at a deed’ that the Kural calls true naan.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a vivid instance of shrinking from wrongdoing, though the text speaks of sin against God, not of shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Prophet (ﷺ) was more shy than a virgin in her separate room. And if he saw a thing which he disliked, we would recognize that (feeling) in his face.”
islam.explanation: Abu Sa'id describes the Prophet's haya' as deeper than a secluded maiden's, and as showing on his face at anything objectionable.
islam.tie_back: The hadith brings together the two kinds of shame the Kural separates: a maiden's bashfulness and a good person's recoil from what is wrong.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it fits the Kural's contrast closely, though it praises both kinds of shame rather than ranking them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is a good sign in a person that he is one who experiences shame. Others say: Any person who experiences shame will not quickly sin”
judaism.explanation: Reading Exodus 20:17 (‘that His fear may be upon your faces’) as shame, the baraita teaches that shame leads to fear of sin.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values shame because it holds a person back from wrong deeds.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 20a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (bold-face markup removed); a near one-to-one match on shame as a brake on sin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the treasure of conscience? There is the case where a disciple of the noble ones feels shame at [the thought of engaging in] bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counts hiri, shame at misconduct of body, speech and mind, among the seven noble treasures.
buddhism.tie_back: It defines shame exactly as the Kural does: shrinking from wrong action.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.6, Dhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; almost one-to-one, and the body-speech-mind triad even matches Kesikan's gloss.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins before the Guru the soul obtains humiliation; feeling humiliated, he will leave off all blameable occupations, and apply himself to praiseworthy occupations”
jainism.explanation: Among the exertions in righteousness, garhā, owning one's faults before the teacher, produces a humbling shame that turns a person away from blameworthy acts.
jainism.tie_back: For the Jain monk as for the Kural, the valuable shame is the one that makes a person drop blameworthy deeds.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (footnote markers removed); a strong fit on shame turning one from blameable acts, framed as monastic confession rather than a general virtue.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector tells Andromache he cannot hang back from the fighting, because he would feel deep shame (aidos) before the Trojan men and long-robed women if he shrank from battle like a coward.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, aidos is the feeling that keeps a hero from a base act even when safety tempts him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector's aidos, like the Kural's naan, is shame at a deed and not mere shyness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage and not checked against a live text; Hector's shame is about public honour in war, which is narrower than the Kural's moral sense.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says shame (aidos) is a kind of fear of disrepute, more a feeling than a virtue. It suits the young, who still go wrong. A decent person should not need it, because he should not do disgraceful things in the first place.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle places shame in actions: it is felt for voluntary bad acts, and its value lies in steering us away from them.
philosophy.tie_back: He agrees with the Kural that real shame is about deeds, but he ranks it below virtue, where Valluvar treats it as an ornament of the noble.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live translation; a close match on shame as a response to deeds, though Aristotle values it less highly.

kurals.tamil:
ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல
நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Oonudai echcham uyirkkellaam veralla
naanudaimai maandhar sirappu.
kurals.meaning: Food, clothing and the other necessities are common to every living being; what sets good people apart is a sense of shame.
kurals.elementary: A puppy eats, a bird sleeps, and you eat and sleep too. So what makes a person special? Valluvar says it is the little voice that says “that would be wrong, I'd be ashamed to do it.” Animals don't have that voice. People do.
kurals.university: Oon (ஊண், 'food'), udai (உடை, 'clothing') and echcham (எச்சம், 'the remainder', i.e. the other bodily needs) are veralla (வேறல்ல, 'not different') for all uyir (உயிர், 'living beings'). By contrast naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, 'the possession of shame') is maandhar sirappu (மாந்தர் சிறப்பு, 'the distinction of humans'). Kesikan and Varadarasanar take the first line to cover all beings and sets of people. Pappaiah narrows the contrast: food and clothing are common to all people, while shame distinguishes the good. Kalaignar explains naanudaimai as avoiding what others condemn. The kural thus makes shame the defining mark of the human, an idea that echoes widely in Indian (Hitopadesha) and Greek (Protagoras) ethics. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha says that eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals. Dharma is the one extra thing that marks out humans, and without it a person is the same as a beast.
hinduism.explanation: This well-known Sanskrit maxim sets the bodily needs shared by all creatures against the moral sense that only humans have.
hinduism.tie_back: Its structure matches the Kural's exactly: common bodily needs in the first line, and in the second the one quality that makes a person truly human, here dharma and in the Kural shame.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Introduction (Prastāvikā), verse beginning āhāra-nidrā-bhaya-maithunaṃ ca (verse numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse whose numbering differs by edition, not checked against a live translation; a near-identical structure, with dharma in place of shame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.”
christianity.explanation: In Genesis the first humans, once their eyes are opened, feel a shame no animal feels and cover themselves.
christianity.tie_back: The verse treats shame as a uniquely human awareness, as the Kural does, though in Genesis it comes with the Fall.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a real link to shame as a distinctively human trait, but the context is guilt after disobedience rather than praise of shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every religion has its distinct characteristic, and the distinct characteristic of Islam is modesty.”
islam.explanation: The hadith names haya', modesty or shame, as the distinguishing character of Islam.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shame the hallmark that sets a people apart.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com, which grades this chain Da'if (weak); the thematic fit on shame as a distinguishing mark is strong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three distinguishing marks of this nation, the Jewish people. They are merciful, they are shamefaced, and they perform acts of kindness.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud attributes to David the teaching that being shamefaced is one of the three marks that identify the people of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a sense of shame is the distinctive quality of the people who have it.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 79a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (bold markup removed; ‘the Jewish people’ is the translator's gloss); a close fit, though it marks one nation rather than humanity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern. If these two bright qualities did not guard the world, there would be no recognition of ‘mother’ here... The world would be immersed in promiscuity, like rams with goats, roosters with pigs, or dogs with jackals.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that conscience (hiri) and concern (ottappa) are what separate human society from the indiscriminate life of animals.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point almost exactly: without shame, humans would be no different from other creatures.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (middle list abridged with an ellipsis); a near one-to-one match on shame as what distinguishes humans from animals.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching holds that a human birth is valuable not for what it shares with other births but for the chance it gives for restraint and the Law.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds what is special about being human in moral restraint rather than in bodily life.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial fit, since it speaks of self-control and the Law rather than of shame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Prometheus myth told in Plato's Protagoras, humans have fire and crafts but keep destroying one another, so Zeus sends Hermes to give every person aidos (shame) and dike (justice). Anyone who cannot share in them is to be put to death as a plague on the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the myth, shame is the gift that turns clever animals into people who can live together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shame, not the means of bodily survival, the defining human excellence.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live translation; a very close structural match, with fire and crafts in the role of the Kural's food and clothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Life seems to be common even to plants, but we are seeking what is peculiar to man. Let us exclude, therefore, the life of nutrition and growth. Next there would be a life of perception, but it also seems to be common even to the horse, the ox, and every animal.”
philosophy.explanation: In his function argument, Aristotle sets aside the life of nourishment and of sensation, which humans share with plants and animals. He looks for what is proper to man alone and finds it in rational, virtuous activity.
philosophy.tie_back: The argument has the Kural's shape, setting aside the needs shared by all living things to find what marks out the good human. Valluvar finds that mark in shame where Aristotle finds it in reason.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7, 1097b-1098a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book I ch. 7). Partial match: the structure is very close, but the distinguishing quality differs. Aristotle names rational activity rather than shame, and elsewhere (IV.9) says shame is not a virtue.

kurals.tamil:
ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம் நாண்என்னும்
நன்மை குறித்தது சால்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Oonaik kuriththa uyirellaam naanennum
nanmai kuriththadhu saalpu.
kurals.meaning: Just as every living being dwells in a body of flesh, perfect nobility dwells in the good quality called shame.
kurals.elementary: A snail lives in its shell and a turtle lives in its shell; they can't live without them. Valluvar says goodness lives inside shame the same way. If you take away a person's shame, their goodness has no home left.
kurals.university: The kural builds an exact parallel. Uyir ellaam oonaik kuriththa (உயிரெல்லாம் ஊனைக் குறித்த): all lives have the body of flesh (ஊன்) as their seat. Saalpu (சால்பு, 'fullness of noble character', the virtue treated in ch. 99, Saanraanmai) has as its seat the nanmai (நன்மை, 'goodness') called naan. The verb kuriththal ('to aim at, to take as one's place') is repeated in both lines. Kesikan presses the image further: as lives never willingly leave their body, saalpu never leaves shame. Kalaignar renders saalpu as maanbu ('dignity'). Pope's ‘perfect virtue ever dwells with shame’ keeps the doubled structure. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…gentleness; modesty; steady determination; vigor; forgiveness; fortitude; cleanliness; and freedom from envy and from the passion for honor – these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists hrīḥ, modesty, among the qualities that make up the ‘divine endowment’ (daivī sampad).
hinduism.tie_back: For the Gita as for the Kural, modesty is part of the seat of a perfected character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (opening of the list elided); modesty is one quality among twenty-six, not the single dwelling-place of virtue the Kural describes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?”
christianity.explanation: Paul pictures the body as the dwelling of the Spirit, and calls believers to purity because of who lives in them.
christianity.tie_back: The verse matches only the Kural's dwelling-place image (a body housing what is highest), not its claim about shame.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a next-best match that parallels the abode imagery but says nothing directly about shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Faith (Belief) consists of more than sixty branches (i.e. parts). And Haya … is a part of faith.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts haya', the sense of shame and modesty, as an inseparable branch of faith.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural seats saalpu in shame, the hadith makes shame part of the very body of faith.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the translator's long parenthetical gloss on haya' elided); a strong fit on shame as constitutive of a higher whole.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When pride cometh, then cometh shame; But with the lowly is wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs holds that wisdom dwells with the tzenu'im, the modest or lowly, while pride ends in disgrace.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the highest human excellence in modesty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good fit on excellence dwelling with modesty, though ‘shame’ here means disgrace, not the virtue of shame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Difficult is life for the modest one who always seeks purity, is detached and unassuming, clean in life, and discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists modesty first among the traits of the one who pursues purity and discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse ties modesty to the full set of noble qualities, much as the Kural seats saalpu in shame.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 245 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it links modesty with purity and discernment, but it lacks the Kural's body-and-soul analogy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The body is the boat, life is the sailor, and the Circle of Births is the ocean which is crossed by the great sages.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi and Gautama, the body is the vessel in which the jiva (life) dwells and travels across samsara.
jainism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's first-line image of life housed in flesh, though not the claim that nobility is housed in shame.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match on the dwelling image only, with no Jain text found that equates shame with the seat of virtue.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar calls Aidos (Shame or Reverence) the daughter of Prometheus (Forethought). She is a goddess who gives men excellence and joy, and when forgetfulness clouds the mind she slips away.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek religious imagination, Aidos is a divine power with whom excellence (arete) comes and goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats shame as the place where excellence lives, so that losing it means losing excellence.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified against a live text; the genealogy is well attested, but the link to excellence is interpretive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza grants that shame is not a virtue, since it is a kind of pain, but says it is good insofar as it shows that the person feeling it wants to live honourably. In the same way, pain is good insofar as it shows the injured part is not yet putrefied.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, shame is a sign that the desire for an honourable life is still present.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats shame as evidence that goodness is still at home in a person.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Proposition 58, Scholium (tr. R.H.M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live text; it shares the idea of shame as the seat or sign of goodness, but Spinoza is more ambivalent than the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு அஃதின்றேல்
பிணிஅன்றோ பீடு நடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aniandro naanudaimai saandrorkku ahdhindrel
piniandro peedu nadai.
kurals.meaning: Is not a sense of shame the jewel of the noble? Without it, is not their proud, stately walk a sickness?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a champion who wins a race and then struts around boasting and laughing at everyone else. It spoils everything, like a sickness. But a champion who wins and stays kind and modest shines like someone wearing a beautiful necklace. Modesty is that necklace.
kurals.university: Two rhetorical questions with ‘andro’ (அன்றோ, ‘is it not?’) frame the kural. Naanudaimai is ani (அணி, 'ornament, jewel') to the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfected'). Without it (ahdhu indrel), their peedu nadai (பீடு நடை, 'gait of eminence, proud bearing') is pini (பிணி, 'disease'). Varadarasanar reads the disease as the proud walk itself. Pappaiah, more pointedly, says it is a disease to those who must watch it. Kalaignar glosses naan here as inward remorse for a wrong done. Pope: ‘without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.’ Thirukkural.net prints a final full stop that ytamizh.com omits; the words are otherwise identical, so the difference is only punctuation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Right after listing modesty among the divine qualities, the Gita lists pride and conceit among the demonic ones.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita sets modesty against pride the same way the Kural does, and treats pride as a corruption of nature, much like the Kural's ‘disease’.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it captures the pride-versus-modesty contrast, but not the image of modesty as an ornament.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that their true jewellery is an inner, meek and quiet spirit, not gold or fine clothes.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: a humble spirit is the real ornament.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on modesty as ornament, though addressed to wives in its context rather than to the noble in general.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets outward clothing and adornment beneath the garment of righteousness (libas al-taqwa).
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names an inner moral quality as a person's best adornment.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good fit on virtue as adornment, though the verse speaks of righteousness generally rather than shame specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the arrogant is headed for Gehinnom and the blushing for the garden of Eden.”
judaism.explanation: Judah ben Tema contrasts the brazen-faced, who end in Gehinnom, with the shamefaced, who reach Eden.
judaism.tie_back: The same contrast as the Kural: the blushing are adorned, while the proud bearing leads to ruin.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:20 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a direct match on pride versus shame, with eschatological stakes the Kural does not use.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be proud of birth, of wealth or clan, and to despise one's own kinsmen — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the causes of a person's decline, the Buddha names arrogance about birth, wealth and clan.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that eminence carried without humility turns into a ruin.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 1.6, Parabhava Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the danger of pride, but not the positive image of modesty as an ornament.

jainism.quote_or_event: Bahubali stands so long in motionless meditation that vines climb his body, yet omniscience does not come. His sisters, the nuns Brahmi and Sundari, tell him to come down from the elephant of pride, since he still refuses to bow to younger brothers who became monks before him. When he lets go of that pride and takes his first step to go and honour them, kevala-jnana dawns.
jainism.explanation: In Jain narrative, even the greatest austerity is blocked by pride, and true greatness appears only when humility returns.
jainism.tie_back: Bahubali's lofty stance without humility is the Kural's ‘stately walk’ that becomes a sickness.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5 (tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in the Adipurana tradition
jainism._accuracy_note: A well-attested Jain story, paraphrased without checking the Johnson translation in this session; Svetambara and Digambara versions differ in detail.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe boasts that with her many children she is greater than the goddess Leto, who has only two. Apollo and Artemis kill all her children, and the grieving Niobe is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Niobe's hubris, pride without restraint or reverence, brings ruin on her whole house.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her boasting is the Kural's stately walk without modesty, and it ends in a fatal sickness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth, not verified against a live text; it fits the danger of pride, while the Kural's image of shame as an ornament is only implied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's chariot allegory the noble white horse is a lover of honour joined with temperance and modesty, and needs only a word of command. The dark horse is a companion of insolence and pride, and barely yields to whip and goad.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the well-ordered soul as led by a modest, honour-loving nature, and the disordered soul as driven by arrogance.
philosophy.tie_back: The modest horse wears the Kural's jewel; the proud horse is the Kural's sickness of pride.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Jowett, not verified live in this session; a good fit on modesty versus pride.

kurals.tamil:
பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் நாணுக்கு
உறைபதி என்னும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirarpazhiyum thampazhiyum naanuvaar naanukku
uraipadhi ennum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Those who feel ashamed of another's disgrace as much as of their own are the ones the world calls the very home of shame.
kurals.elementary: When your friend gets caught being unkind, do you just laugh? Or do you feel a little hot in the face, as if it were you? Valluvar says the people who feel ashamed even when someone else does wrong are the ones whose hearts are truly good.
kurals.university: Pirar pazhi (பிறர்பழி, 'the blame or disgrace of others') and tham pazhi (தம்பழி, 'one's own disgrace') are set side by side. The one who naanuvaar (நாணுவார், 'feels shame') at both is called by the world naanukku uraipadhi (நாணுக்கு உறைபதி, 'the dwelling-place of shame itself'). Kesikan stresses that such a person weighs the two kinds of blame equally. Pappaiah reads ‘not only one's own but also others' blame’. Pope's couplet, ‘Who feel ashamed for others' guilt as for their own’, follows the same line. The kural extends shame from a private brake to a shared moral sensitivity, which fits the Kudiyiyal's concern with the honour of family and community. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the dice-hall of the Mahabharata, while elders like Bhishma and Drona stay silent as Draupadi is humiliated, the young Kaurava prince Vikarna rises alone. He is stung by the shame the assembly is bringing on itself, and he protests that the wrong being done must be named.
hinduism.explanation: Vikarna feels the disgrace of his own kin and elders as if it were his own, and cannot keep silent.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's naanukku uraipadhi: ashamed of others' wrongdoing as much as of his own.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), Vikarna's protest
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a live translation; Vikarna's motive is presented as outrage at injustice, which fits shared shame only partly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that when any believer is made to stumble, he himself burns with distress.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's ideal, Paul feels another's moral fall as his own.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on sharing in others' failures, though it speaks of distress and indignation rather than shame as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the community as one body, so that one member's affliction is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: This solidarity underlies the Kural's ideal of feeling another's disgrace as one's own.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a sound fit on shared feeling, though it concerns suffering in general rather than shame at blame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to Thee, my God; for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our guiltiness is grown up unto the heavens.”
judaism.explanation: Ezra, who had not himself transgressed, tears his garments and confesses the people's sin as ‘our iniquities’, blushing before God.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal exactly: an innocent man ashamed of others' guilt as if it were his own.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on shame taken on for others' guilt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha criticises the habit of airing others' faults while hiding one's own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person does the opposite: he weighs others' blame and his own alike and feels both.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 252 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a next-best match that warns against an unequal treatment of faults rather than commending shared shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: Umasvati teaches four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness (maitri) toward all living beings, joy (pramoda) in the virtuous, compassion (karunya) for those in distress, and equanimity (madhyasthya) toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: These four reflections widen the Jain practitioner's moral feeling to include the condition of others.
jainism.tie_back: They share the Kural's outward-turned sensitivity, though Jainism asks for compassion and equanimity toward others' faults, not shame at them.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.6 (Svetambara numbering; 7.11 in Digambara numbering), tr. Nathmal Tatia
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against Tatia in this session; a next-best match, since no Jain text found here commends feeling shame for others' blame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Paris shrinks back from facing Menelaus, his brother Hector rebukes him bitterly. Paris's cowardice is a disgrace to their father, their city and all their people, and Hector feels that disgrace keenly as his own family's.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector cannot treat his brother's shame as someone else's business; it stains the whole house.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's ideal, Hector feels his kinsman's disgrace as his own.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live text; it fits shared family shame, but Hector's response is more anger than self-implicating shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith observes that we blush for the impudence and rudeness of another person even when he himself seems to have no sense of how improperly he is behaving.
philosophy.explanation: Smith's account of sympathy explains how we come to feel a shame that properly belongs to someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘ashamed of others' blame as of one's own’, explained through the psychology of sympathy.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1.10 (1759)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known line, not verified live in this session; a near-direct match on vicarious shame.

kurals.tamil:
நாண்வேலி கொள்ளாது மன்னோ வியன்ஞாலம்
பேணலர் மேலா யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanveli kollaadhu manno viyangnaalam
paenalar melaa yavar.
kurals.meaning: The truly great would not want even the whole wide world if it meant giving up the hedge of shame; shame, not the world, is what guards them.
kurals.elementary: A garden has a fence so goats can't come in and eat the flowers. Valluvar says good people keep a fence of shame around their hearts. Even if someone offered them the whole world, they wouldn't trade away that fence.
kurals.university: Naan veli (நாண்வேலி, 'the hedge or fence that is shame') is the central image. The melaayavar (மேலாயவர், 'the superior ones') will not paenal (பேணல், 'cherish, desire') the viyan gnaalam (வியன்ஞாலம், 'vast world') without taking (kollaadhu) that hedge; manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Kesikan and Pappaiah, in the line of Parimelazhagar, take it to mean that the great choose shame rather than the wide world as their protection. Varadarasanar reads it as saying the great would not want to live in the wide world without the protecting hedge of shame. Pope gives a more poetic turn: ‘For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain’ unless the hedge stays intact. Sivayogi Sivakumar's modern reading, that one cannot rise to greatness without the hedge, is a minority interpretation. The text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama offers the boy Nachiketas long life, cattle, horses, gold, wide lands and every pleasure if only he will stop asking about what lies beyond death. Nachiketas refuses: let Yama keep the horses, the dance and the song; he will hold to the one boon he asked for.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad praises the one who turns down the whole pleasant world for the sake of what is truly good (śreyas).
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas, like the Kural's great ones, would not take the vast world at the price of what guards his soul.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; it fits the refusal of the world, but what Nachiketas chooses is knowledge, not shame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that winning the whole world is worthless if it costs a person his soul.
christianity.tie_back: The same trade the Kural rejects: the vast world is not worth losing the inner safeguard.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close structural match (the world against an inner good), though ‘soul’ is broader than shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Once Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) passed by an Ansari (man) who was admonishing his brother regarding Haya'. On that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, ‘Leave him as Haya' is a part of faith.’”
islam.explanation: A man scolds his brother for being too bashful, presumably because it cost him worldly advantage, and the Prophet defends the bashfulness as part of faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's great ones, the Prophet would rather keep haya' than gain worldly advantage by giving it up.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the worldly-cost context comes from the commentators, so the fit with the Kural's ‘world versus hedge’ is partly interpretive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Tradition is a fence to the Torah; Tithes a fence to wealth, Vows a fence to abstinence; A fence to wisdom is silence.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva describes protective practices as fences (seyag) that guard a deeper good.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's image of shame as a fence guarding the good person.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (opening clause omitted); it matches the protective-fence image but does not name shame among the fences.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who in the world is a man constrained by conscience, who awakens to censure like a fine stallion to the whip? Those restrained by conscience are rare”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures hiri (conscience, shame) as the restraint that keeps a person on the path, like a thoroughbred that answers to a mere touch of the whip.
buddhism.tie_back: Shame here is the guard of the noble person, as in the Kural's hedge.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.18, Hiri Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (line breaks joined); a good fit on shame as protective restraint, though there is no ‘world versus shame’ trade-off.

jainism.quote_or_event: “…by hearing and understanding which the monks will reach a high degree of self-discipline, of Samvara, and of contemplation, will be well protected (by the three Guptis), will guard their senses, guard their chastity, and will thus never be remiss”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sets out ten protective conditions around celibacy. Later Jain tradition calls these the nava vāḍa, literally ‘nine fences’, of brahmacarya.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's naan veli, these are deliberate fences that guard a monk's purity.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 16, prose introduction (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (italic diacritics flattened); it matches the protective-fence idea, but the fences guard chastity rather than being shame itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Through twenty years and the pressure of many powerful suitors who could give her a new household and status, Penelope keeps her faith with absent Odysseus. She puts them off with the trick of weaving and unweaving Laertes' shroud.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's guarded fidelity, which Homer praises as her renown, protects her and her house better than any worldly alliance could.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Kural's noble one, who prefers the guard of honour to the gains the world offers.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live; it fits a self-guarding honour preferred over worldly gain, but Homer frames it as fidelity rather than shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus tells someone urging him to get money for his friends that if it can be had while keeping his self-respect, fidelity and magnanimity, he will get it. But if he is asked to lose his own proper good so that others can gain what is not truly good, the request is foolish and unjust.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, a person's aidos (self-respect, modesty) and good faith are worth more than any external gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's great ones, Epictetus will not trade the guard of his own integrity for the goods of the world.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live translation in this session; a good structural match, with aidos among the goods Epictetus protects.

kurals.tamil:
நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால்
நாண்துறவார் நாணாள் பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanaal uyiraith thurappar uyirpporuttaal
naanthuravaar naanaal pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who live by shame will give up their life for its sake, but will never give up shame to save their life.
kurals.elementary: Some heroes in stories are asked to do something really wrong, like betray a friend, or else they'll be hurt. And they say no, even though it's scary. Valluvar says people with real shame would rather lose everything than do something shameful.
kurals.university: The kural is built as a chiasmus. Naanaal uyiraith thurappar (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர், 'for shame's sake they renounce life') is mirrored by uyir poruttaal naan thuravaar (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார், 'for life's sake they do not renounce shame'). Naan aalpavar (நாணாள்பவர், 'those who wield or rule by shame') are its subject. Kesikan frames it as a dilemma: when shame and life cannot both be kept, the noble let life go. Kalaignar substitutes maanam (honour), linking the kural to ch. 97 (Maanam), where similar sentiments appear (e.g. kural 969 on the yak that dies on losing its hair). Pope: ‘The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that for an honoured man, disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ranking exactly: losing one's shame or honour is worse than losing one's life.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a close match, though the Gita speaks of public reputation (akīrti) while the Kural speaks of inner shame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to value faithfulness above bodily survival.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks bodily life below the inner good one must never surrender.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the life-below-integrity ranking, but its motive is fear of God rather than shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: Pressed to give in to seduction or face prison, Joseph (Yusuf) chooses the dungeon over a shameful act.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf would give up his freedom rather than his modesty, the Kural's choice made concrete.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit, though the threat is prison rather than death.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idol worship, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed, a person must let himself be killed rather than transgress (yehareg ve'al ya'avor).
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law sets certain boundaries that may not be crossed even to save one's life.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's principle as law: life is given up before the deepest integrity is.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known ruling, not verified live in this session; a close fit, though it is framed as divine command rather than shame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his monks that even if bandits were to saw them limb from limb with a two-handled saw, anyone who let his mind turn to hatred would not be following his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: The Saw Simile demands that a monk keep his inner discipline even at the cost of a terrible death.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks keeping one's moral self above keeping one's body alive.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (The Simile of the Saw)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live; it fits the life-below-integrity theme, but what is preserved is goodwill, not shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati rebukes the monk Rathanemi when he tempts her to break their vows, telling him death would be better than such shamelessness. Shamed, he returns to the Law.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati states the Kural's principle outright: better to die than to give up shame for the sake of this life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); the same verse appears in Dasavaikalika Sutra 2
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed); a near-direct match, framed as monastic vows.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Troy falls, the captive princess Polyxena is led to be sacrificed at Achilles' tomb. She refuses to be held and goes freely to her death rather than live as a slave, and even as she falls she takes care to fall modestly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides presents Polyxena as choosing an honourable death over a shameful life and keeping her modesty to the end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyxena is the Kural's naan-aalpavar: she gives up life for shame's sake and never gives up shame for life's sake.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live; a strong fit, though the setting (human sacrifice in war) is far from the Kural's ethical register.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial Socrates says that a man worth anything should not weigh the chances of living or dying. He should ask only whether he is acting rightly or wrongly. Achilles chose death rather than disgrace.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates refuses to save his life by giving up philosophy or begging shamefully.
philosophy.tie_back: His stance is the Kural's: life may be given up, integrity may not.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live text in this session; a close match, with Socrates himself invoking the shame of disgrace.

kurals.tamil:
பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது தான்நாணா னாயின்
அறம்நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirarnaanath thakkadhu thaannaanaa naayin
aramnaanath thakkadhu udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: If a person feels no shame at what would make others ashamed, then virtue itself will be ashamed of him and leave.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone does something so rude that everyone watching feels embarrassed, but he just grins. Valluvar says that even Goodness itself would feel embarrassed to be his friend and would quietly walk away from him.
kurals.university: The kural personifies aram (அறம், 'virtue, dharma'). If one does not feel shame (thaan naanaan aayin) at what is pirar naanath thakkadhu (பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது, 'fit to make others ashamed'), then he udaiththu (உடைத்து, 'has in him') something aram naanath thakkadhu, at which virtue itself would blush. There are two lines of interpretation. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say virtue, ashamed, abandons him. Pappaiah and Kesikan say he harbours a fault at which virtue is ashamed. Kesikan's gloss reads the first line as ‘what onlookers would blame’. Pope's ‘Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!’ follows the abandonment reading. The repeated naanath thakkadhu across both lines is characteristic Valluvar wordplay. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are demoniac do not know what is to be done and what is not to be done. Neither cleanliness nor proper behavior nor truth is found in them.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes the āsuric person as one from whom right conduct and truth have departed.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the shameless person of the Kural, from whom virtue has withdrawn.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.7 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it captures virtue's absence, though not the image of shamelessness causing it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who glory in what ought to shame them.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural's shameless ones, unashamed of what should shame anyone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on inverted shame, without the image of virtue departing.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the sayings of the early Prophets which the people have got is: If you don't feel ashamed … do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet quotes the ancient maxim that once shame is gone, nothing holds a person back from anything.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shamelessness the moment moral restraint is lost.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the translator's parenthetical gloss elided); a near-direct match on shamelessness as the loss of all moral restraint.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They shall be put to shame because they have committed abomination; Yea, they are not at all ashamed, Neither know they how to blush; Therefore they shall fall among them that fall”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah condemns a people who commit abominations without the least blush.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's shameless man, who will not blush at what should shame him, and who falls.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match on the inability to blush, with divine punishment in place of virtue's departure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the shameless, brazen as a crow, find life easy precisely because nothing restrains them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's person who feels no shame where others would.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 244 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on shamelessness, though it lacks the image of virtue itself being ashamed.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins to oneself the soul obtains repentance, and becoming indifferent by repentance he prepares for himself an (ascending) scale of virtues, by which he destroys the Karman resulting from delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Nindā, inwardly condemning one's own faults, is what keeps a soul climbing the scale of virtues.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point from the other side: without inner shame at wrongdoing, virtue has nowhere to stand.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed); an inverse, partial fit, since it praises self-reproach rather than picturing virtue leaving the shameless.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And then Aidos and Nemesis … with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod foresees that when men grow utterly shameless, the goddesses Shame and Righteous Indignation will abandon the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's image exactly: a divine personified virtue, ashamed, departs from the shameless.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 197-200 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, Theoi Classical Texts Library)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com (the translator's bracketed gloss elided); a near one-to-one match, with a personified virtue leaving the shameless.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Theophrastus sketches the Shameless Man (anaischyntos), who cheats the people he owes, borrows from the person he has just defrauded, and treats anything as acceptable as long as he gains by it, untroubled by what others think.
philosophy.explanation: Theophrastus' character sketch shows how one who feels no shame drifts from every decent norm.
philosophy.tie_back: It portrays the man the Kural warns of, who does unblushingly what would shame anyone else.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified live; it fits the type of the shameless man, but it is satire rather than ethical theory.

kurals.tamil:
குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் நலஞ்சுடும்
நாணின்மை நின்றக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kulanjudum kolgai pizhaippin nalanjudum
naaninmai nindrak kadai.
kurals.meaning: A lapse in conduct burns away the good name of one's family; but once shamelessness takes hold, it burns away every good thing a person has.
kurals.elementary: If you break a rule once, people might think less of your family for a while. But if you stop caring at all whether you do wrong, it's like a fire that keeps spreading and burns up everything good about you.
kurals.university: The kural ranks two fires with the same verb, sudum (சுடும், 'burns, destroys'). If kolgai (கொள்கை, 'one's settled conduct', glossed by the commentators as ozhukkam) pizhaippin (பிழைப்பின், 'should fail'), it burns the kulam (குலம், 'family, lineage'). But naaninmai (நாணின்மை, 'shamelessness') nindra kadai (நின்றக் கடை, 'once it becomes settled') burns all nalam (நலம், 'every good'). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the second fire as more total than the first; Kesikan says the first ruins only the family's standing while the second consumes everything. Kalaignar connects the lines: failing to feel shame at one's lapse lets ruin spread. Pope: ‘'Twill race consume if right observance fail; 'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.’ The text (with the doubled consonant in நின்றக் கடை) is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With the destruction of the dynasty, the eternal family tradition is vanquished, and thus the rest of the family becomes involved in irreligion.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna fears that once a family's dharma breaks down, adharma overtakes the whole line.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita shares the Kural's concern that a lapse in conduct ruins the kulam.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.39 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a good match for the first line on family ruin, though it is Arjuna's argument, which Krishna later answers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes deceivers whose conscience has been cauterised until it no longer feels.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of burning (sudum) for what happens when shame is lost.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the burning image is shared, but in Paul the conscience is burned, while in the Kural shamelessness burns everything else.

islam.quote_or_event: “Haya' (pious shyness from committing religeous indiscretions) does not bring anything except good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that haya' produces only good.
islam.tie_back: The positive counterpart of the Kural: where shame brings only good, shamelessness burns all good away.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (including the source's spelling ‘religeous’); a strong inverse match on shame as the source of all good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one who does not have the capacity to be shamefaced, it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats shamelessness as evidence that a person's lineage lacks the formative experience of Sinai.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links a person's shamelessness to the standing of his whole lineage.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 20a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (bold markup removed); a good match on shamelessness and lineage, from the same passage used for kural 1011.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man's wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that persistent wrongdoing uproots a person's own foundations, here and now.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's fire of shamelessness, settled misconduct destroys every good a person has.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 246-247 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it fits total ruin from settled wrongdoing, but it names the five precepts rather than shamelessness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, refusing Rathanemi's advances, guards both her family's honour and her own virtue, and reminds him that those born into a noble family must not fall.
jainism.tie_back: The episode joins the Kural's two concerns: conduct guards the kulam, and shame guards one's whole good.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.40, with 22.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good fit on conduct preserving clan honour and virtue, from the same lecture used for kural 1017.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Oresteia the crimes of Atreus, including the feast he served his brother Thyestes, bring a curse on the house that passes from generation to generation: Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia, his murder by Clytemnestra, and Orestes' revenge.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek tragedy, one shameless outrage blights an entire family line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line on a tragic scale: a breach of conduct burns the kulam.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live; it fits family ruin, but the Greek curse works through inherited guilt rather than a lack of shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And does not the legislator and every one who is good for anything, hold this fear in the greatest honour? This is what he terms reverence, and the confidence which is the reverse of this he terms insolence; and the latter he always deems to be a very great evil both to individuals and to states.”
philosophy.explanation: The Athenian Stranger defines shame as the fear of being thought evil for a dishonourable word or deed. Its opposite, a shameless boldness, he calls a very great evil for persons and cities alike.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato, like the Kural, treats the loss of shame as a ruin that goes deeper than any single lapse.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Laws Book I). Strong match on shamelessness as a grave evil; Plato does not draw the Kural's contrast between harm to the family's name and harm to all one's goods.

kurals.tamil:
நாண்அகத் தில்லார் இயக்கம் மரப்பாவை
நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanagath thillaar iyakkam marappaavai
naanaal uyirmarutti atru.
kurals.meaning: The movements of people with no shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet jerked about on strings to fool onlookers into thinking it is alive.
kurals.elementary: Have you seen a puppet show? The puppet dances and waves, but it isn't really alive; someone is pulling strings. Valluvar says a person with no shame inside is like that: moving around, but with nothing real inside.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a pun on naan (நாண்), which means both ‘shame’ and ‘cord, string’ (as in a bowstring). Those who lack naan agaththu (நாண் அகத்து, 'shame within') move like a marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll, puppet') that, by naanaal (நாணால், 'by means of strings'), uyir maruttum (உயிர்மருட்டும், 'deceives people into thinking it has life'). Kesikan glosses the strings as the yantra cords of a mechanical doll, and Varadarasanar and Pappaiah describe a doll worked by rope to look alive. So the shameless are alive in appearance only, moved by outside pulls rather than by an inner moral life. The wordplay (shame in the first line, string in the second) is often singled out as one of Valluvar's finest. Pope: ‘'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Lord is situated in everyone's heart, O Arjuna, and is directing the wanderings of all living entities, who are seated as on a machine, made of the material energy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes embodied beings as mounted on a mechanism (yantra), moved about by māyā.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a being moved like a mechanical figure, though the Gita applies it to all embodied life, not to the shameless.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a next-best match that shares only the mechanical-puppet image, not the moral point.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Sardis that it looks alive but is spiritually dead.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's puppet: an appearance of life with no living core.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on seeming alive while dead within, though not specifically about shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the hypocrites as impressive in appearance but hollow, like propped-up pieces of timber.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an and the Kural reach for the same image: wooden figures that only look alive, standing for people empty within.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a very close image match, aimed at hypocrisy rather than shamelessness as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalmist mocks idols of silver and gold: they have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, feet but do not walk. Those who make them, and trust in them, become like them.
judaism.explanation: Psalm 115 contrasts lifeless crafted figures with the living God, and warns that their devotees grow equally lifeless.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a person without a living inner core as no better than a crafted figure that only mimics life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; it shares the lifeless-figure image, but its target is idolatry rather than shamelessness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Behold this body — a painted image, a mass of heaped up sores, infirm, full of hankering — of which nothing is lasting or stable!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the body a ‘painted image’ (cittakata bimba), a dressed-up figure without lasting substance.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a decorated figure that only looks alive and lasting.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 147 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a next-best match on the image only, since the verse concerns impermanence, not shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain doctrine sharply separates jiva, the conscious soul whose mark is awareness, from ajiva, non-sentient matter. The Uttaradhyayana's final lecture sets out this division, and karma is pictured as ajiva matter that binds the jiva and drives its movements through samsara.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, movement driven by karmic matter rather than by the awakened soul is not true living.
jainism.tie_back: This loosely parallels the Kural's shameless puppet, whose motion comes from strings rather than an inner moral life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); Tattvartha Sutra 2.8 (consciousness as the mark of the soul)
jainism._accuracy_note: Interpretive paraphrase of doctrine, not verified line by line; a next-best match, since no Jain text found here uses the puppet image for the shameless.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hephaestus is attended by handmaidens made of gold that look like living young women. They move, speak and help him as if they had minds of their own, though they are his crafted works.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's golden automata are the classic Greek image of a made thing that imitates life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's marappaavai in myth: figures that fool the eye into seeing life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live; it matches the image of lifelike automata, but Homer passes no moral judgment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Athenian imagines each of us as a puppet of the gods, pulled by inner cords of pleasure, pain and fear. We should follow only the one soft golden cord of reason and law, and resist the hard iron ones.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, a person who is jerked about by appetites rather than guided by the golden cord lives a puppet's life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's puppet image applied to ethics: without an inner guiding cord (for Valluvar, naan), a person is moved only by strings.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified live in this session; a strong image-and-meaning match, and Plato's ‘cord’ even echoes the Kural's pun on naan as ‘string’.
